title: C: Array Functions That Accept Input
description: Writing functions that read keyboard input and store it directly into an array.
congratsText: Well done. You can now write a function that fills an array from input, explain why it works without a return, and reuse the same shape elsewhere.
objectives: Write a function that fills an array from user input
Trace how a smaller size limits which slots get filled
Explain why array parameters update main() without a return
Apply the same fill-loop shape to a new array or a new rule
recap: void means nothing is handed back; the function still changes the array directly.
size controls how many slots the loop asks for; skipped slots keep old leftover memory.
Array parameters share the same memory as the caller's array; plain int parameters only get a copy.
The same loop shape — void, array, size, scanf with & — reuses cleanly across different arrays and rules.

sections.title: A Function That Fills an Array

chunks.text: The first word of the function is its return type. void fillScores(...) means nothing is handed back to whoever called it.

check.question: What does the word void at the front of a function tell you?
options: It only takes whole numbers in

chunks.text: Inside the loop, scanf("%d", &arr[i]); needs the & so it knows the address to store into, not just a value.

check.question: What does the & in front of arr[i] give scanf?
options: The value already inside that slot

chunks.text: The call fillScores(scores, 5); runs the whole loop once. Since arr and scores point at the same memory, main() sees the typed numbers right away.

check.question: After fillScores(scores, 5); runs, does main() need to do anything else to see the typed numbers?
options: Yes, it must return them first

quiz.question: The user types 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in order. What does this print?
options: 5, the size that was passed in
An address, since arr[] holds one

chunks.text: The size you pass decides how many times the loop asks for input. Same array, smaller size, fewer questions asked.

check.question: The array holds 5 slots but you call fillScores(scores, 3). How many numbers does it ask for?

chunks.text: Slots the loop never reaches keep whatever was already in memory — not zero, not blank, just leftover bytes from before.

check.question: fillScores(scores, 3) runs. What is inside scores[4] afterward?

chunks.text: Two separate arrays can share the exact same function. fillAges(ages, 5); reuses the identical loop shape fillScores used, just on a different array.

check.question: Does fillAges need its own new loop logic, different from fillScores?
options: Yes, every array needs its own logic

quiz.question: Type the number this prints.

sections.title: Why This Works Without a Return

chunks.text: An array parameter like int arr[] is really the same address as the array in main() — there is only one array, viewed from two names.

check.question: Inside fillScores, is arr[] a brand new copy of the array?
options: No, it's the same memory as scores
Yes, a fresh copy is made

chunks.text: A plain int score parameter is different: C copies the value in, so changes made inside the function never reach main().

check.question: You pass a plain int into a void function and change it inside. Does main()'s copy change too?
options: No, only the local copy changes

chunks.text: This quietly compiles either way — right or wrong, the Compile Log stays clean. A clean build only means the code is legal, not that it does what you meant.

check.question: Your program builds with no errors. Does that prove the array got filled correctly?
options: Yes, a clean build proves it

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a function that fills an array of ages.

chunks.text: Add one more rule and the shape barely changes: fillPositive(arr, size) keeps asking until the number typed is zero or higher.

check.question: Why can fillPositive reuse the same void, array, size shape as fillScores?
options: The core pattern (loop + scanf + &) doesn't change
Rules always require a brand new return type

chunks.text: The & is still doing the exact same job here — giving scanf an address to write into, rule or no rule.

check.question: Does adding the zero-or-higher rule change why & is needed?
options: No, & still means: store the address here
Yes, rules need scanf to skip the &

chunks.text: If you call fillPositive(prices, 3) on a 5-slot array, prices[3] and prices[4] are left holding whatever was already there — the same leftover-memory gap as before.

check.question: fillPositive(prices, 3) runs on a 5-slot array. What's inside prices[4] afterward?
options: Leftover memory, same as any skipped slot

quiz.question: The user types -5, 20, 15, 8, 3 in that order (the -5 gets rejected). What does this print?
